Percentile-based ranks against others; an absolute measure does not.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: To do with government taxation and spending.
practiceSentences: The fiscal year runs from July to June here.
What fiscal measures could reduce water waste?
Fiscal policy works through taxes and spending, not interest rates.
The fiscal cost of the subsidy was never published.
Fiscal concerns tax and spending; monetary concerns money supply.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: To do with money supply and interest rates.
practiceSentences: Monetary policy raised borrowing costs across the region.
What monetary tools does a central bank actually hold?
Monetary decisions reach farmers through the price of a loan.
The monetary and fiscal responses pulled in opposite directions.
Monetary policy is set by a central bank; fiscal policy by a government.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: Working through the buying and selling of goods between countries.
practiceSentences: A trade-based solution asks who will buy, not who will give.
Is a trade-based approach more durable than aid?
A trade-based scheme survives only while the market does.
They preferred trade-based agreements to a single donation.
Trade-based exchanges goods; aid-based transfers them.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: The supply of workers and the demand for them.
practiceSentences: The labour-market tightened once the mine reopened.
What does this labour-market offer a school leaver?
A labour-market is local long before it is national.
Migration reshaped the labour-market within one season.
The labour-market matches workers to work, well or badly.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: How geography shapes power and relations between countries.
practiceSentences: The geopolitics of a shared river outlasts any single government.
What geopolitics surrounds control of this strait?
Geopolitics explains why a resource is never only a resource.
Water scarcity turned an engineering problem into geopolitics.
Geopolitics concerns power across borders; domestic policy stops at them.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: To do with genes and what is inherited through them.
practiceSentences: The drought-tolerant variety carries a genetic advantage.
What genetic difference explains the shorter stem?
A genetic change is inherited; a learned one is not.
They screened the seed stock for genetic diversity.
Genetic concerns the genes; environmental concerns everything else.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: The way traits and characteristics are passed from parents to their children.
practiceSentences: Heredity explains why the two herds differ in size.
What does heredity contribute to drought tolerance?
Heredity passes on instructions, not experiences.
Farmers used heredity long before anyone could explain it.
Heredity is the passing on; genetics is the study of how.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: One of the alternative forms a gene can take.
practiceSentences: Each parent contributes one allele for the trait.
Which allele is dominant in this variety?
An allele can be carried without ever being expressed.
The rare allele survived in one isolated population.
A gene is the location; an allele is the version found there.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: A large region defined by its climate and the life it supports.
practiceSentences: The savanna biome stretches across several countries.
Which biome does this district sit in?
A biome is defined by climate first and by borders never.
Rainfall and temperature between them decide the biome.
A biome is regional; an ecosystem can be one pond.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: Planned to achieve a long-term aim.
practiceSentences: Planting the windbreak was strategic rather than urgent.
What strategic reason lies behind this reservoir?
A strategic decision accepts a cost now for a gain later.
Their strategic reserve of seed carried them through two poor years.
Strategic looks at the long aim; tactical handles the immediate problem.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: Able to be moved and used in a different situation.
practiceSentences: The method proved transferable to three neighbouring districts.
Which findings here are transferable, and which are local?
A transferable skill survives a change of employer.
Not every transferable idea should be transferred.
Transferable moves between contexts; contextual does not.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: Given and received in return by both sides.
practiceSentences: The two villages have a reciprocal arrangement over grazing.
Is this obligation reciprocal or one-sided?
A reciprocal agreement survives because both sides need it.
Their reciprocal trade in seed outlasted three droughts.
In mathematics, the reciprocal of a number is one divided by it.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: Keeping a healthy relationship with screens and online life.
practiceSentences: Digital-wellbeing is about how time online feels, not only how long it is.
What digital-wellbeing habits actually survive a busy week?
Digital-wellbeing treats attention as something worth protecting.
The school's digital-wellbeing policy covers staff as well as pupils.
Digital-wellbeing concerns the effect; screen time only counts the minutes.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: Recognising what could go wrong before it does.
practiceSentences: Risk-awareness turned a near miss into a changed procedure.
What risk-awareness does working near an open well require?
Risk-awareness is noticing the hazard, not fearing it.
Their risk-awareness training used real incidents from the district.
Risk-awareness sees the danger; risk management does something about it.

words.group: Words: resources, money and how they are measured
words.childMeaning: A planned approach to keeping people healthy in mind and body.
practiceSentences: The co-operative's wellbeing-strategy began with shorter harvest shifts.
What belongs in a wellbeing-strategy for seasonal workers?
A wellbeing-strategy that names no budget is a wish.
Their wellbeing-strategy was written with the workers, not for them.
A wellbeing-strategy plans; wellbeing is the outcome it aims at.

words.group: Grammar: turning a verb into a noun, and verbs without tense
words.childMeaning: Turning a verb or adjective into a noun.
practiceSentences: "Decide" becomes "decision" through nominalisation.
Which nominalisation hides who acted in this sentence?
Nominalisation lets a writer describe an action without naming the actor.
Official reports use nominalisation to sound neutral.
Nominalisation makes a noun; a verb keeps the action visible.

words.group: Grammar: turning a verb into a noun, and verbs without tense
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb form that shows no tense or subject agreement.
practiceSentences: In "to reduce waste", "to reduce" is non-finite.
Which non-finite form opens this sentence?
A non-finite verb cannot form a sentence on its own.
Infinitives, gerunds and participles are all non-finite.
A finite verb carries tense; a non-finite one does not.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: To do with the non-living parts of an environment.
practiceSentences: Temperature, light and soil are abiotic factors.
Which abiotic factor limits growth on this slope?
An abiotic factor shapes what can live somewhere at all.
The survey recorded abiotic conditions before counting a single species.
Abiotic means non-living; biotic means living.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: To do with the living parts of an environment.
practiceSentences: Predators and competitors are biotic factors.
What biotic pressures act on this population?
A biotic factor is another organism affecting yours.
Biotic and abiotic factors together decide who survives.
Biotic covers everything alive, including what is too small to see.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Working with a whole habitat rather than one species at a time.
practiceSentences: An ecosystem-based plan protects the river as well as the fish.
Why is an ecosystem-based approach slower to show results?
Ecosystem-based management treats the system as the unit.
The reserve adopted an ecosystem-based policy after the first plan failed.
Ecosystem-based means the whole habitat is the thing being managed.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Founded on how living things relate to each other and their surroundings.
practiceSentences: An ecology-based design works with the slope instead of against it.
What would an ecology-based farm look like here?
Ecology-based thinking asks what else a change will touch.
The scheme is ecology-based and deliberately unhurried.
Ecology-based starts from relationships; engineering starts from structures.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: The movement of heat by a flowing liquid or gas.
practiceSentences: Convection carries warm air up the valley each afternoon.
How does convection form a cloud?
Convection needs something that can flow.
The kettle heats by convection long before the water boils.
Convection moves the heat with the fluid; conduction passes it through a solid.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: A state of balance where opposing forces cancel out.
practiceSentences: The population reached an equilibrium after four seasons.
What would upset the equilibrium of this pool?
An equilibrium is not stillness; it is change that balances.
Removing one predator ended the equilibrium within a year.
An equilibrium can be stable or precarious, and looks identical until it is tested.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: To investigate something closely, or an instrument for doing so.
practiceSentences: The team probed the sediment for traces of the old shoreline.
What would you probe first?
To probe is to keep asking after the obvious answer.
She pushed the probe into the soil and read the temperature.
A probe investigates; a survey counts.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: To repeat something exactly so the result can be checked.
practiceSentences: Another team could not replicate the finding.
How would you replicate this study on a different river?
A result nobody can replicate is not yet a result.
They replicated the count three times in one week.
To replicate is to repeat the method; to copy is to repeat the answer.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: To identify what is wrong from the signs available.
practiceSentences: The ranger diagnosed the die-off as a water problem.
How would you diagnose the cause of this decline?
To diagnose is to name a cause, not just a symptom.
She diagnosed the fault in the pump within minutes.
Diagnosing comes before treating, and is the harder half.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Depending on the surrounding situation for its meaning.
practiceSentences: The reading is contextual: the same figure means different things in wet and dry seasons.
What contextual information does this graph leave out?
A contextual judgement cannot be transferred whole to another site.
She added contextual notes so the numbers could be read later.
Contextual means it depends on the setting; absolute means it does not.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Based on what has been observed or measured.
practiceSentences: The claim is empirical, so it can be checked.
What empirical evidence supports this?
An empirical answer beats a confident one.
Their empirical work took six seasons of counting.
Empirical rests on observation; theoretical rests on reasoning.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Considering something as a whole rather than in parts.
practiceSentences: A holistic survey records the soil as well as the birds.
What would a holistic view of this valley include?
A holistic approach resists solving one problem into another.
The report took a holistic view and was twice as long.
Holistic looks at the whole; reductive takes it apart.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Not certain, and open to being changed.
practiceSentences: The conclusion is tentative until a second season confirms it.
Is that a tentative finding or a settled one?
A tentative claim is honest about how much it knows.
They published a tentative figure and invited correction.
Tentative means held lightly, not held weakly.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Based on reason or logic; sensible.
practiceSentences: Panic spreads quickly, so leaders must stay rational when plans go wrong.
A rational flood plan weighs the cost of barriers against the price of doing nothing.
Is it rational to plant thirsty lawns in a town that faces water shortages every summer?
"Stay rational," said the chairperson gently; "anger fills the room but empties the budget."
I try to make rational choices about transport, though I admit the bus's warmth sways me in January.

words.group: Words: living systems and the balance they keep
words.childMeaning: Seeming reasonable or likely to be true.
practiceSentences: Adam's theory about the coded message sounded plausible until Rohan spotted a contradiction in it.
Does an explanation become plausible simply because a confident speaker repeats it often enough?
"Your excuse is plausible," said the librarian, "but the return date on this book says otherwise."
I try to test every plausible claim I read online before repeating it to my friends.
A plausible story still needs evidence before you believe it.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ity
words.childMeaning: Making something official by setting it out in fixed rules.
practiceSentences: The formalisation of the grazing agreement ended a century of argument.
What does formalisation gain over a shared understanding?
Formalisation makes a practice enforceable and less flexible at once.
Their formalisation of the boundary took three years of surveying.
Formalisation writes the rule down; custom leaves it unwritten.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ity
words.childMeaning: The breaking of something whole into separated pieces.
practiceSentences: Habitat fragmentation isolates populations that used to mix.
What causes fragmentation of a forest this size?
Fragmentation can leave the total area unchanged and the habitat ruined.
A single road caused more fragmentation than the farming beside it.
Fragmentation divides what was continuous; destruction removes it.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: The whole zone of the Earth where living things exist.
practiceSentences: The biosphere reaches from deep ocean trenches to high mountain air.
How thin is the biosphere compared with the planet?
The biosphere is a layer, not a place.
Everything alive has always lived inside the biosphere.
The biosphere covers all life; a biome is one region of it.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: Considering a whole habitat rather than single species.
practiceSentences: An ecosystem-level survey counts the soil as well as the birds.
Why does ecosystem-level thinking change what gets protected?
An ecosystem-level change can follow the loss of one species.
They set ecosystem-level targets instead of counting one animal.
Ecosystem-level looks at the whole system; species-level at one part of it.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: To do with feeding levels in a food chain.
practiceSentences: Each trophic level passes on about a tenth of its energy.
Which trophic level does this predator occupy?
A trophic cascade begins when one level is removed.
The wolves' return caused a trophic change reaching the riverbanks.
Trophic concerns who eats whom, level by level.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: The study of the great plates that make up the Earth's surface.
practiceSentences: Tectonics explains why the lakes lie in a line.
What does tectonics tell us about this valley's future?
Tectonics works in centimetres a year and mountains a million.
The rift's tectonics is still separating the two plates.
Tectonics studies the plates; geology studies the rock they carry.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: How fast a plant makes food from light, water and air.
practiceSentences: The photosynthetic-rate falls once the leaves lose water.
What limits the photosynthetic-rate on a bright cold morning?
A photosynthetic-rate is limited by whichever factor is scarcest.
They measured the photosynthetic-rate by the oxygen released.
The photosynthetic-rate is a speed; photosynthesis is the process.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: The size of something, especially measured on a scale.
practiceSentences: An earthquake of magnitude seven releases far more than one of six.
What is the magnitude of this change in real terms?
The magnitude scale is logarithmic, so each step is a tenfold jump.
She reported the magnitude and the direction separately.
Magnitude is size alone; a vector adds direction to it.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: A quantity that has size but no direction.
practiceSentences: Temperature is a scalar; wind is not.
Which of these measurements is scalar?
A scalar needs one number and no arrow.
Speed is a scalar and velocity is its vector partner.
A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has direction too.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: Using quantities that carry both size and direction.
practiceSentences: A vector-based model tracks where the ash will travel, not just how much.
Why must a wind forecast be vector-based?
A vector-based calculation cannot ignore direction and still be right.
Their vector-based map showed the current's strength and its bearing.
Vector-based carries direction; scalar-based does not.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: The set of all points that satisfy a given condition.
practiceSentences: The locus of points a fixed distance from the centre is a circle.
What locus does this rule describe?
A locus is a shape defined by a condition rather than drawn.
She sketched the locus before naming it.
In biology, a locus is a gene's position on a chromosome.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: The study of the relationships between angles and sides in triangles.
practiceSentences: Trigonometry gives the cliff's height without anyone climbing it.
What trigonometry would you use to find this distance?
Trigonometry turns one angle and one length into everything else.
Surveyors used trigonometry to map the rift long before satellites.
Trigonometry measures triangles; geometry studies shape more widely.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: To do with shape, size and the relationships between them.
practiceSentences: The crystal's geometric structure repeats in every direction.
What geometric pattern does this honeycomb follow?
A geometric argument can prove what measurement only suggests.
She described the terraces in geometric terms.
Geometric concerns shape; arithmetic concerns number.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: Being identical in shape and size.
practiceSentences: Congruence means one shape fits exactly onto the other.
How would you prove congruence between these triangles?
Congruence survives turning and flipping; it does not survive resizing.
The two crystal faces showed exact congruence.
Congruence is identical; similarity keeps the shape and changes the scale.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: A point where two or more lines or edges meet.
practiceSentences: A cube has eight vertices and twelve edges.
Which vertex is furthest from the base?
A vertex is a corner, named precisely.
She labelled each vertex before measuring the angles.
The plural of vertex is vertices.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: Careful, thorough, and following the method exactly.
practiceSentences: A rigorous survey repeats the count in three seasons.
What makes this study rigorous rather than merely long?
Rigorous work is designed to survive somebody trying to break it.
Their rigorous method found an error in their own first year.
Rigorous follows the method; thorough only covers everything.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: Done according to a plan, in an orderly and repeatable way.
practiceSentences: A systematic survey walks the same transect every time.
What does a systematic search of this valley involve?
A systematic method can be repeated by somebody who was not there.
The team's systematic recording made twenty years of data comparable.
Systematic follows a plan; thorough merely misses nothing.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: Helping to identify what something is or what is wrong.
practiceSentences: Lichen is a diagnostic sign of clean air.
What diagnostic feature separates these two species?
A diagnostic feature identifies; a common one does not.
She used leaf shape as the diagnostic test in the field.
Diagnostic identifies the case; descriptive only reports it.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: An individual's own capacity to choose and to act.
practiceSentences: Personal-agency is what a rule either protects or removes.
What personal-agency does a volunteer actually hold here?
Personal-agency depends on real options, not only on permission.
The scheme was redesigned to increase personal-agency in the field teams.
Personal-agency belongs to one person; collective agency belongs to a group.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: The power to make your own choices and take action for yourself.
practiceSentences: The community was given agency over how the reserve is managed.
Should local people have agency over conservation decisions?
Agency means the power to act, not merely to be consulted.
Imani argued that agency without funding is a courtesy.
Agency is the capacity to act; an agency is an organisation.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: A short sharp saying that states a truth.
practiceSentences: "Nature does nothing in vain" is an aphorism.
Which aphorism opens the conservation report?
An aphorism has to be short enough to remember and true enough to keep.
She closed the talk on an aphorism and sat down.
An aphorism states a truth; a proverb carries the weight of custom.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: A sudden drop from something lofty to something trivial.
practiceSentences: The speech ended in bathos: the future of the planet, and then the raffle.
Where does the bathos fall in this paragraph?
Bathos is usually accidental, which is why it is funny.
The documentary's grand music over a puddle was pure bathos.
Bathos falls flat by accident; irony means to.

words.group: Words: the shape of the natural world
words.childMeaning: The release of strong feeling through watching or reading something.
practiceSentences: The film's ending offered catharsis rather than an answer.
What catharsis does a tragedy provide its audience?
Catharsis is a release, not a solution.
The community's shared grief found catharsis in the ceremony.
Catharsis empties the feeling; consolation replaces it.

words.group: Grammar: balance in a sentence, and the two aspects of a verb
words.childMeaning: Repeating a grammatical structure to give writing balance.
practiceSentences: "We came, we saw, we counted" uses parallelism.
Where does parallelism strengthen this passage?
Parallelism makes a list feel deliberate rather than accidental.
Breaking parallelism halfway through a sentence jars the reader.
Parallelism repeats a structure; repetition repeats the words.

words.group: Grammar: balance in a sentence, and the two aspects of a verb
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb form that presents an action as completed.
practiceSentences: "She has counted the nests" is perfective.
Which perfective form suits this report?
The perfective presents an action as finished, whenever it happened.
Field notes mix perfective and progressive without noticing.
The perfective closes an action; the progressive leaves it running.

words.group: Words: people, work and how a country is run
words.childMeaning: A country's right to govern itself without outside control.
practiceSentences: Sovereignty means the decisions are made at home.
Does joining a treaty reduce sovereignty?
Sovereignty is claimed by a state and recognised by others.
The islands' sovereignty was disputed for a century.
Sovereignty is authority; independence is the condition of having it.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: All the chemical processes that keep a living thing going.
practiceSentences: Training slowly changes an athlete's metabolism.
How does metabolism differ between rest and effort?
Metabolism is what turns food into movement and heat.
Her metabolism recovered faster than the coach expected.
Metabolism builds up and breaks down at the same time.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: To do with the glands that release hormones into the blood.
practiceSentences: The endocrine system controls growth and recovery.
Which endocrine gland releases adrenaline?
The endocrine system works slowly, through the bloodstream.
Endocrine signals reach every cell rather than one target.
The endocrine system uses chemicals; the nervous system uses electricity.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: The body's ability to resist a particular disease.
practiceSentences: Immunity can come from having the illness or from a vaccine.
How long does immunity to this virus last?
Immunity is specific: it protects against one thing, not everything.
Hard training can lower immunity for a day or two.
Immunity also means being protected from a rule or a penalty.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: To do with the cells that living things are made of.
practiceSentences: Recovery happens at a cellular level long before it is felt.
What cellular change does endurance training cause?
Cellular damage from hard effort is repaired during sleep.
The study measured cellular oxygen use during a sprint.
Cellular also describes a phone network built from cells.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: The study of how features are passed from parents to offspring.
practiceSentences: Genetics explains part of an athlete's ceiling, not all of it.
What does genetics contribute to endurance?
Genetics loads the dice; training rolls them.
She studied genetics after a season of injuries.
Genetics is the study; genes are what it studies.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: A change in the genetic instructions of a living thing.
practiceSentences: A mutation can be harmful, helpful, or make no difference at all.
How often does a mutation occur naturally?
Most mutations do nothing an athlete would ever notice.
A single mutation explains this rare advantage in altitude.
Mutation supplies the variation that selection then acts on.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Based on the collecting and study of numerical data.
practiceSentences: The claim rests on a statistical difference, not a visible one.
Is this a statistical result or a single good day?
A statistical finding says how likely a pattern is to be chance.
The federation published a statistical review of the season.
Statistical means from the numbers; anecdotal means from a story.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: A relationship in which two things change together.
practiceSentences: There is a correlation between training hours and finishing times.
What correlation does this graph show?
Correlation is not causation, which is the most repeated warning in statistics.
A strong correlation can still be a coincidence.
A correlation can be positive, negative, or absent.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: A value below which a given percentage of results fall.
practiceSentences: Her time put her in the ninetieth percentile.
Which percentile marks the qualifying standard?
A percentile says where you stand, not how fast you are.
The fiftieth percentile is the median.
A percentile ranks; a percentage measures.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Describing the range covering the middle half of the data.
practiceSentences: The interquartile range ignores the fastest and slowest quarters.
What is the interquartile range of these times?
The interquartile range is not disturbed by one freak result.
She compared the interquartile ranges rather than the extremes.
Interquartile means between the quarters, which is exactly what it measures.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Choosing part of a group to learn about the whole.
practiceSentences: Sampling every tenth runner gave a fair picture.
What sampling method did the study use?
Careless sampling produces confident nonsense.
Random sampling avoids the choices a person would make.
Sampling saves time; bad sampling wastes everything after it.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Involving two variables at once.
practiceSentences: A scatter graph is bivariate by definition.
What bivariate relationship is this study testing?
Bivariate data pairs each measurement with another.
She plotted the bivariate data and the pattern appeared.
Bivariate is two variables; univariate is one.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Strong, and able to hold up under pressure or scrutiny.
practiceSentences: The finding is robust across three different seasons.
Is this conclusion robust enough to publish?
A robust result survives being tested by somebody hostile.
Their robust defence conceded twice in twenty matches.
Robust withstands; rigid resists until it breaks.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: So convincing or interesting that it holds your attention.
practiceSentences: The evidence for the new method is compelling.
What makes this argument compelling rather than merely loud?
A compelling case anticipates the strongest objection.
Her compelling final lap changed how the race is remembered.
Compelling persuades; forceful only pushes.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid.
practiceSentences: After months of missed training sessions, the team's relegation began to feel inevitable.
Was the champion's defeat inevitable once the injury started affecting her landing?
"Mistakes are inevitable," the coach reassured us, "but repeating them is a choice."
I used to think losing to the city schools was inevitable, until our new goalkeeper proved otherwise.
Calling something inevitable afterwards is easier than predicting it before.

words.group: Words: the body, the data and the podium
words.childMeaning: Necessary to make something complete.
practiceSentences: Recovery is integral to a training plan, not an extra.
Is the warm-up integral or optional?
An integral part cannot be removed without changing the whole.
Her role became integral to how the team defended.
Integral means built in; important only means it matters.

words.group: Word building: -ity and -ation
words.childMeaning: The range of things something is able to do.
practiceSentences: The archive's functionality grew with every year of cataloguing.
What functionality does a public record actually need?
Functionality is what it does; usability is whether anyone can.
They added search functionality and readership doubled.
Functionality lists the capabilities; design decides how they feel.

words.group: Word building: -ity and -ation
words.childMeaning: Establishing who or what something is.
practiceSentences: Identification of the author took three years and one letter.
What identification does this document require?
Identification is a claim that has to be evidenced.
The photograph allowed positive identification of the site.
Identification names the thing; description only characterises it.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: A policy of extending a country's power over other territories.
practiceSentences: Imperialism redrew the borders this region still lives with.
How did imperialism justify itself to the people at home?
Imperialism outlives the empire that practised it.
The museum's new wing examines imperialism without softening it.
Imperialism is the policy; colonialism is settling and ruling the land.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: A political belief that the nation's interests come before all others.
practiceSentences: Nationalism can unite a country and can also define who is excluded from it.
How does nationalism differ from simple pride in a place?
Nationalism ranks the nation above other loyalties, which is its whole claim.
The movement's nationalism won independence and then narrowed.
Patriotism loves a country; nationalism ranks it against others.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: The principle that government power is limited by a constitution.
practiceSentences: Constitutionalism means the ruler is also under the law.
What does constitutionalism require of a court?
Constitutionalism limits power in advance rather than punishing it after.
The new republic's constitutionalism was tested within a decade.
Constitutionalism binds the government; democracy chooses it.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: A system dividing power between central and regional governments.
practiceSentences: Federalism leaves education to the regions and defence to the centre.
What does federalism solve that a single government cannot?
Federalism accepts that one rule will not suit every province.
Their federalism survived because both levels had real money.
Federalism divides power by territory; separation of powers divides it by function.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Rule that demands obedience and allows little dissent.
practiceSentences: Authoritarianism concentrates decisions and discourages questions.
What makes authoritarianism attractive during a crisis?
Authoritarianism trades argument for speed, and keeps the trade.
The press laws were the first sign of authoritarianism.
Authoritarianism restricts dissent; totalitarianism tries to reach every part of life.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: The belief that deep and fundamental change is needed.
practiceSentences: Her radicalism looked extreme in her lifetime and ordinary afterwards.
What distinguishes radicalism from mere impatience?
Radicalism goes to the root, which is what the word means.
The movement's radicalism frightened the very people it would help.
Radicalism seeks fundamental change; reformism works within the system.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Concern for human welfare, especially in crisis and suffering.
practiceSentences: Humanitarianism sends help without asking which side anyone is on.
What limits does humanitarianism place on its own actions?
Humanitarianism relieves suffering; it does not settle its cause.
Her humanitarianism took her to three famines in one decade.
Humanitarianism responds to need; charity responds to appeal.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Working through agreements between many countries at once.
practiceSentences: Multilateralism is slow, and it binds more parties than a bargain between two.
Why does multilateralism struggle when one member withdraws?
Multilateralism trades speed for legitimacy.
The treaty was multilateralism at its most patient.
Multilateralism involves many states; bilateralism involves two.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Operating across national borders rather than within one.
practiceSentences: The campaign became transnational within a year.
What makes a problem transnational rather than foreign?
A transnational body answers to no single government.
Transnational trade routes predate most of the borders they cross.
Transnational crosses borders; international is between the states themselves.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Decided by those entitled to vote rather than by appointment.
practiceSentences: An electorate-based council answers to the district every four years.
Is an electorate-based system always the fairest one?
An electorate-based body can be removed, which is its point.
They replaced appointed governors with an electorate-based assembly.
Electorate-based means chosen by voters; merit-based means chosen on qualification.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: A quality belonging to something, or to name what caused a result.
practiceSentences: Scientists attribute the falling fish populations to warmer seas and decades of relentless overfishing.
Which attribute of a great leader matters most during a crisis: honesty or vision?
"Patience is the attribute I value most," said the beekeeper as she calmed the restless hive.
I would attribute my improved grades to steady revision rather than last-minute cramming.
To attribute a result is to name its cause, which is a claim needing evidence.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: To find something out with certainty.
practiceSentences: Historians could not ascertain the date from the letter alone.
How would you ascertain who wrote this?
To ascertain is to establish, not to assume.
She ascertained the facts before repeating any of them.
Ascertain settles a question; speculate leaves it open.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: To settle a dispute by making a binding decision.
practiceSentences: A neutral panel was asked to arbitrate the boundary claim.
Who should arbitrate when both sides distrust the courts?
To arbitrate is to decide; the parties agree in advance to accept it.
The commission arbitrated and both governments complied.
To arbitrate is to decide the matter; to mediate is to help them decide it.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: To help two sides reach their own agreement.
practiceSentences: A neighbouring state offered to mediate between the two governments.
Can you mediate between the director and the writer before things get worse?
To mediate is to hold the room, not to hand down a ruling.
The elder mediated for a week and neither side lost face.
To mediate is to help them agree; to arbitrate is to decide for them.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: To be connected in a way where each affects the other.
practiceSentences: Trade, migration and language interrelate across this whole coast.
How do these two reforms interrelate?
Things that interrelate cannot be reformed one at a time.
Her thesis showed how the three movements interrelate.
To interrelate is mutual; to relate can run one way.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Final and authoritative, settling the question.
practiceSentences: Her biography is still the definitive account.
Is this evidence definitive or merely strong?
A definitive answer closes a question that others reopen anyway.
The definitive edition took forty years to assemble.
Definitive settles it; conclusive only ends this particular argument.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Never having happened before.
practiceSentences: The scale of the migration was unprecedented in the region's records.
Is this genuinely unprecedented, or only unrecorded?
Unprecedented is a claim about the record, not about the world.
The archive showed the event was rare rather than unprecedented.
Unprecedented has no earlier example; unusual merely has few.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Copied from an earlier work and adding little of its own.
practiceSentences: The later speeches were derivative of one famous address.
What makes this work derivative rather than influenced?
Derivative work borrows the form and misses the reason.
Critics called the memorial derivative and the public loved it.
In mathematics, a derivative measures a rate of change.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Working out what is right by thinking it through.
practiceSentences: Moral-reasoning asks for the reason, not only the verdict.
What moral-reasoning lies behind this decision?
Moral-reasoning can reach a conclusion you dislike, which is the test of it.
She traced the leader's moral-reasoning through his letters.
Moral-reasoning weighs right and wrong; legal reasoning weighs what is permitted.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: Applying agreed principles to decide what should be done.
practiceSentences: Ethical-reasoning starts from a principle and tests it against the case.
What ethical-reasoning would justify publishing the letters?
Ethical-reasoning is public: it can be set out and disputed.
The committee's ethical-reasoning was printed alongside its decision.
Ethical-reasoning applies a shared framework; moral-reasoning may be personal.

words.group: Words: power, legacy and how it is judged
words.childMeaning: A person's own sense of their gender.
practiceSentences: Gender-identity is what a person knows about themselves.
How has the language for gender-identity changed in fifty years?
Gender-identity is reported by the person, not assigned by an observer.
The historian was careful about gender-identity when writing of the past.
Gender-identity is internal; a role is what a society expects.

words.group: Grammar: an unfinished action, and clauses that define
words.childMeaning: Describing a verb form showing an action still in progress.
practiceSentences: "She was writing" is progressive; "she wrote" is not.
Which progressive form suits this account?
The progressive leaves an action unfinished at the time described.
Historians use the progressive to place one event inside another.
The progressive keeps an action running; the perfective closes it.

words.group: Grammar: an unfinished action, and clauses that define
words.childMeaning: Describing a clause that identifies which one is meant.
practiceSentences: In "the leader who signed the treaty", the restrictive clause identifies which leader.
Which clause here is restrictive?
A restrictive clause takes no commas, because removing it changes the meaning.
She added commas and turned a restrictive clause into an aside.
A restrictive clause defines; a non-restrictive one merely adds.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: A hope or dream of achieving something in the future.
practiceSentences: Jamal's aspiration to become a pilot began the day he first watched planes from the airport fence.
Does every aspiration need a deadline, or can some dreams stay open-ended?
"Write down one aspiration," said the careers adviser, "then list three steps that lead towards it."
My deepest aspiration is to open a school in my grandparents' village one day.
An aspiration without a first step stays a wish.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Your belief that you can do what a task requires.
practiceSentences: Self-efficacy grows from small successes, not from encouragement.
How does one hard exam affect self-efficacy?
Self-efficacy is about a particular task, not about yourself in general.
Her self-efficacy in mathematics rose the term she stopped guessing.
Self-efficacy is what you believe you can do; confidence is how you feel.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Acting from firm beliefs about right and wrong.
practiceSentences: A principled refusal cost her the contract.
What makes a decision principled rather than convenient?
A principled stand is only tested when it costs something.
He was principled to the point of being difficult.
Principled means guided by principle; stubborn means guided by nothing.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Something you are required to do by duty or agreement.
practiceSentences: The apprenticeship carries an obligation to complete two years.
What obligation does an employer owe a trainee?
An obligation binds whether or not you feel like it.
She met every obligation and resented half of them.
An obligation is owed; a choice is made.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Beliefs about what is right and wrong behaviour.
practiceSentences: The debate turned on morality rather than on law.
Whose morality should a company follow?
Morality asks what ought to be done; law says what must be.
Her morality was formed long before the job tested it.
Morality is the system of belief; ethics is the study of it.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: When prices for things go up, so you need more money to buy the same things.
practiceSentences: When inflation rises sharply, families discover that their weekly wages buy far fewer groceries.
Because of inflation, the same loaf of bread now costs far more than last year.
How does inflation make it harder for families to afford their weekly shopping?
After the drought destroyed the crops, inflation pushed the price of maize far beyond most wages.
I learned that rapid inflation can shrink the value of money almost overnight.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: A system where the government controls important things like schools and hospitals to help everyone equally.
practiceSentences: Under socialism, the community pays together for the hospitals and schools that everyone relies upon.
Under socialism, the government provides services like hospitals so everyone can receive care.
How does socialism try to reduce the gap between the richest and poorest citizens?
Supporters of socialism argue that shared hospitals and schools protect families during a serious crisis.
I compared socialism with capitalism to understand how each system organises a country's economy.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To judge the worth or quality of something carefully.
practiceSentences: The manager appraises each apprentice twice a year.
How would you appraise your own first draft?
To appraise is to judge against a standard, not against a mood.
She appraised the offer for a week before answering.
Appraise is to assess; apprise is to inform, and they are different words.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To judge something again in the light of new information.
practiceSentences: The result made them reassess the whole approach.
When would you reassess this decision?
To reassess is not to admit defeat; it is to use what arrived late.
She reassessed the plan and kept three quarters of it.
Reassessing regularly is cheaper than being wrong for a year.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: To create new ideas, methods, or products.
practiceSentences: Small schools can innovate just as effectively as large, well-funded companies.
What stops a community from choosing to innovate when resources are scarce?
Kofi, you never stop trying to innovate, even with the simplest materials!
Great teams innovate by asking better questions, not by having more money.
To innovate is to put a new idea to work, not merely to have one.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Able to act and decide independently.
practiceSentences: The team was autonomous within an agreed budget.
How autonomous should a first-year apprentice be?
Autonomous means answerable for the decision as well as free to make it.
She wanted an autonomous role and got a lonely one.
Autonomous governs itself; independent is simply not governed by another.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Examining something by breaking it into its parts.
practiceSentences: An analytical approach found the fault in an afternoon.
What analytical skills does this job actually need?
Analytical work separates a problem before solving it.
Her analytical report was longer and far more useful.
Analytical takes apart; holistic looks at the whole.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Using few words to say something clearly.
practiceSentences: Sami trimmed his speech until every point was concise enough to fit the two-minute limit.
Why is a concise headline often more persuasive than a paragraph of detailed explanation?
"Keep your answers concise," the examiner advised, "because rambling responses bury your strongest ideas."
I admire writers who stay concise, since respecting the reader's time is itself a form of clarity.
Their rule was concise: if you cannot cite a source, you cannot repeat the claim.

words.group: Words: work, ambition and the standards you set
words.childMeaning: Allowed by rules or law, or reasonable and justified.
practiceSentences: The company holds a legitimate licence for the work.
Is that a legitimate reason for refusing the request?
A legitimate complaint deserves an answer even when it is inconvenient.
Her legitimate expectation was set out in the contract.
Legitimate can mean lawful, or simply fair enough.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -tion and -ation
words.childMeaning: The reasons given to show that something is right or necessary.
practiceSentences: The novel offers no justification for what its hero does.
What justification does the narrator give for lying?
A justification is offered; whether it holds is a separate question.
Her essay examined the justification rather than the act.
A justification argues it was right; an excuse asks to be forgiven.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -tion and -ation
words.childMeaning: Bringing something up to date with current methods or ideas.
practiceSentences: The modernisation of the theatre kept its walls and changed everything else.
What did modernisation cost the traditions it replaced?
Modernisation is a choice about what to keep, not only what to add.
The publisher's modernisation of the spelling divided readers.
Modernisation updates; restoration returns something to how it was.

words.group: Word building: -ation, -tion and -ation
words.childMeaning: Judging by facts rather than by personal feeling.
practiceSentences: Complete objectivity is a direction to travel in, not a place to arrive.
What threatens objectivity in a first-person account?
Objectivity is easier to claim than to demonstrate.
She separated her objectivity from her sympathy and said so.
Objectivity rests on the evidence; subjectivity rests on the observer.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: The shape a story takes from its opening to its resolution.
practiceSentences: The narrative-arc rises to the storm and falls away in two pages.
What narrative-arc does this folk tale follow?
A narrative-arc is a shape, not a sequence of events.
She mapped the narrative-arc before rewriting the middle.
A narrative-arc is the shape; a plot is what happens.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: The character or manner in which a story is told.
practiceSentences: The narrative-voice is a child's, and the understanding is an adult's.
Whose narrative-voice carries this chapter?
A narrative-voice can be trusted, doubted, or both at once.
Changing the narrative-voice changed which events mattered.
Narrative-voice is who tells it; point of view is what they can see.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: A constructed character a writer speaks through.
practiceSentences: The poet adopts the persona of a soldier who never returned.
What persona does the essayist take on here?
A persona lets a writer say what they could not say directly.
Her public persona and her letters barely resemble each other.
A persona is assumed; a personality is had.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: A narrator whose account the reader learns not to trust.
practiceSentences: The unreliable-narrator contradicts himself on the second page.
How does a reader detect an unreliable-narrator?
An unreliable-narrator makes the reader do the work of judging.
The story only makes sense once you accept the unreliable-narrator.
An unreliable-narrator may be lying, or simply mistaken.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Writing that follows a character's thoughts as they come.
practiceSentences: The chapter is stream-of-consciousness and has almost no full stops.
Why is stream-of-consciousness harder to read aloud?
Stream-of-consciousness reproduces thought rather than reporting it.
She used stream-of-consciousness for the hour before the storm.
Stream-of-consciousness follows the mind; description follows the eye.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: The way one text refers to and depends on others.
practiceSentences: The novel's intertextuality assumes you know the older legend.
What intertextuality does this title set up?
Intertextuality rewards a reader who has read elsewhere.
Her essay traced the intertextuality between three retellings.
Intertextuality is the relationship; an allusion is one instance of it.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: A smaller category within a larger kind of writing.
practiceSentences: Detective fiction is a subgenre of crime writing.
Which subgenre does this story belong to?
A subgenre carries expectations the wider genre does not.
The prize added a subgenre for climate fiction.
A genre is the broad kind; a subgenre is a family within it.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: The set of works a tradition treats as most important.
practiceSentences: The canon changes more often than it admits.
Who decides what enters the canon?
A canon reflects who was reading as much as who was writing.
Three East African novelists entered the canon within a decade.
A canon is what a tradition keeps; a bestseller list is what it buys.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: An extended and surprising comparison running through a work.
practiceSentences: The whole poem rests on a conceit comparing memory to a well.
What conceit holds this piece together?
A conceit is a comparison stretched further than seems wise, on purpose.
Her conceit of the city as a body carried four stanzas.
A conceit is elaborate and sustained; a simile is brief.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: A comparison developed across several lines or a whole text.
practiceSentences: The extended-metaphor of the drought runs to the final page.
What extended-metaphor governs this chapter?
An extended-metaphor has to keep working, line after line.
She built an extended-metaphor from one image in the opening.
An extended-metaphor is sustained; a metaphor may be a phrase.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Working through objects that stand for larger ideas.
practiceSentences: The film's symbolism-based ending refuses to explain itself.
Is this a symbolism-based reading or a literal one?
A symbolism-based interpretation must still fit the words on the page.
Their symbolism-based analysis found three meanings for the river.
Symbolism-based reads objects as standing for ideas; literal takes them as they are.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: What a writer is trying to achieve with a piece of writing.
practiceSentences: The writer-purpose here is to unsettle, not to inform.
What writer-purpose explains this odd opening?
Writer-purpose is inferred from the text, not asked of the author.
Identifying writer-purpose changed how the class read the ending.
Writer-purpose is the aim; effect is what actually happened to the reader.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Technology that lays digital images over the real world.
practiceSentences: The museum's augmented-reality guide rebuilds the ruin as you stand in it.
What can augmented-reality show that a photograph cannot?
Augmented-reality adds to the real scene rather than replacing it.
Their augmented-reality retelling placed the story in the actual street.
Augmented-reality adds to the world; virtual reality substitutes for it.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Using distant servers over a network instead of local machines.
practiceSentences: Cloud-computing let the small studio render a film overnight.
What does cloud-computing cost besides money?
Cloud-computing moves the machine, not the responsibility.
The archive moved to cloud-computing and kept one local copy.
Cloud-computing runs elsewhere; local computing runs on your own device.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: The work of designing, writing and maintaining programs.
practiceSentences: Software-development is mostly reading code somebody else wrote.
What does software-development involve besides writing code?
Software-development spends more time on maintenance than on creation.
Her software-development team was three people and a long list.
Software-development builds the program; web-development builds for the browser.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Building sites and applications that run in a browser.
practiceSentences: Web-development has to work on a phone with a poor signal.
What does web-development assume about the reader's device?
Web-development is designing for a screen you have never seen.
Their web-development kept the storytelling site under one megabyte.
Web-development targets the browser; software-development need not.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Concerned with ideas rather than with particular examples.
practiceSentences: The objection is conceptual: the categories do not hold.
What conceptual problem does this framework have?
A conceptual difficulty survives every new example you add.
She separated the conceptual issues from the practical ones.
Conceptual concerns the idea; empirical concerns the evidence.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Made or treated differently to suit different cases.
practiceSentences: The reading list is differentiated by confidence rather than by age.
How is this task differentiated for a mixed class?
Differentiated work respects a difference instead of ignoring it.
Their differentiated approach gave three routes to the same text.
Differentiated adapts to the case; standardised applies one form to all.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: Having several distinct aspects that all matter.
practiceSentences: The character is multidimensional and never entirely likeable.
What makes this portrayal multidimensional rather than merely detailed?
A multidimensional character resists being summarised in a sentence.
Her multidimensional reading held three interpretations at once.
Multidimensional has several aspects; complicated merely has many parts.

words.group: Words: how a story is built and read
words.childMeaning: To treat something accepted as a question worth examining.
practiceSentences: The essay problematises the idea of a single national story.
What would you problematise in this account?
To problematise is to stop treating something as obvious.
She problematised the word tradition before using it once.
To problematise is to open a question; to criticise is to answer it.

words.group: Grammar: clauses that only add, and turning a sentence around
words.childMeaning: Describing a clause that adds information without identifying.
practiceSentences: In "the novel, which sold poorly, is now a classic", the clause is non-restrictive.
Which clause here is non-restrictive?
A non-restrictive clause takes commas and can be removed.
Dropping the commas turned a non-restrictive clause into a defining one.
A non-restrictive clause adds; a restrictive one identifies.

words.group: Grammar: clauses that only add, and turning a sentence around
words.childMeaning: Reversing the usual order of words in a sentence.
practiceSentences: "Never had she seen such a storm" uses inversion.
Where does inversion appear in this opening?
Inversion slows a reader and marks the line as deliberate.
The poet used inversion to place the verb last.
Inversion reorders for effect; a question reorders by rule.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: The art of using language to persuade.
practiceSentences: The speech was fine rhetoric and thin on evidence.
What rhetoric does this headline use?
Rhetoric is a skill, and a skill can be used either way.
She studied rhetoric to become harder to persuade.
Rhetoric is the craft of persuasion; propaganda is persuasion with the other side removed.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A mild word used in place of a blunt or unpleasant one.
practiceSentences: Letting staff go is a euphemism for dismissing them.
Which euphemism is this report hiding behind?
A euphemism softens the sentence and hides the fact.
She replaced every euphemism with the plain word and the piece changed entirely.
A euphemism is polite; a lie is not, but the distance can be short.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Using humour to expose and criticise something.
practiceSentences: The satirical column is the most read page in the paper.
Is this piece satirical or simply rude?
A satirical article attacks a target, not merely a mood.
Satirical writing needs its readers to know what is being mocked.
Satirical mocks in order to criticise; comic only wants a laugh.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: An imitation of a style, made to be funny.
practiceSentences: The sketch was a parody of the evening news.
What is this parody actually imitating?
A parody has to copy well before it can mock.
Their parody of the advert was shared more widely than the advert.
A parody imitates a style; a caricature exaggerates a person.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A picture or description that exaggerates features for effect.
practiceSentences: The caricature gave the minister an enormous chin.
Which feature does this caricature exaggerate?
A caricature works because it is recognisable and unfair.
The article was a caricature of a complicated argument.
A caricature exaggerates what is there; a fabrication invents it.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: The meaning underneath what is actually said.
practiceSentences: The subtext of the statement was that nobody would be blamed.
What is the subtext of this apology?
Subtext is what a careful reader hears and a quick one misses.
She read the subtext before she finished the first paragraph.
The text is what is written; the subtext is what is meant.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Misinformation is false or inaccurate information that is spread, often without the person realising it is wrong.
practiceSentences: Sami learned to recognise misinformation by asking where a story first appeared.
Why does misinformation spread faster than a careful correction ever does?
That post is pure misinformation, Kian!
The class discussed how misinformation can damage trust between neighbours.
Every time you ask the five questions, you break one link in the chain of misinformation.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Information describing other information, such as when a file was made.
practiceSentences: The photograph's metadata gave the date and the place.
What metadata does this document carry?
Metadata often reveals more than the file it describes.
Journalists checked the metadata before believing the image.
Metadata is data about data, which is why it is easy to forget.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Describing software whose code anyone may read and change.
practiceSentences: The tool is open-source, so anyone can inspect what it does.
Why does open-source matter for trusting a program?
Open-source is not the same as free of charge.
They chose an open-source encyclopedia over a closed one.
Open-source publishes the code; proprietary keeps it hidden.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Information, often one-sided or misleading, spread to promote a particular cause.
practiceSentences: The word propaganda originally just meant the spreading of information.
Can an advert cross the line into propaganda without anyone noticing?
Nora explained how propaganda gained its negative meaning during the twentieth century.
The class studied propaganda techniques used in political campaigns.
Bright posters and catchy slogans made the propaganda easy to swallow.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: The act of working to make a change in society or to help a cause.
practiceSentences: Her activism began with a letter to the local paper.
What activism has changed a law you benefit from?
Activism is patient work that occasionally looks sudden.
Online activism reaches further and commits less.
Activism seeks change; reporting seeks to describe it.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: All the people entitled to vote in an election.
practiceSentences: The electorate grew by forty thousand this year.
What does the electorate actually want here?
An electorate is a group defined by a right, not by an opinion.
Newspapers claim to speak for an electorate that never asked them to.
The electorate votes; the government governs.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: A penalty imposed to make a country or person obey.
practiceSentences: The sanctions were lifted after the agreement was signed.
What sanction would actually change this behaviour?
A sanction is meant to cost more than the behaviour is worth.
Trade sanctions hurt the people before they reach the government.
Sanction is its own opposite: it also means to give official approval.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Based on personal feelings rather than on facts.
practiceSentences: A review is subjective and should say so.
Is that judgement subjective or can it be tested?
A subjective opinion is not thereby worthless.
She separated the subjective paragraphs from the reported ones.
Subjective comes from the person; objective from the thing.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Having a mistake or weakness that makes something less than perfect.
practiceSentences: The survey was flawed because only readers replied.
What makes this method flawed rather than merely limited?
A flawed study can still point in the right direction.
The argument is flawed at its second step.
Flawed means it has a fault; false means it is wrong.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: Open to more than one meaning.
practiceSentences: The headline was ambiguous, and probably on purpose.
Which word makes this sentence ambiguous?
An ambiguous statement lets a speaker deny either reading.
She rewrote the ambiguous clause into two plain ones.
Ambiguous offers two clear meanings; vague offers none.

words.group: Words: how news persuades, and how to read it
words.childMeaning: To question something closely and searchingly.
practiceSentences: Interrogate the source before you quote it.
How would you interrogate this claim?
To interrogate a statistic is to ask who counted, and how.
She interrogated the data and found the missing month.
To interrogate is to question hard; to interview is to let somebody speak.

words.group: Word building: -al, -ation and -ence
words.childMeaning: Ready to work, or to do with day-to-day running.
practiceSentences: The recording studio became operational three months late.
What operational problems does a touring band face?
An operational decision is made daily; a strategic one rarely.
Their operational costs were higher than the instruments.
Operational concerns the running; strategic concerns the direction.

words.group: Word building: -al, -ation and -ence
words.childMeaning: Reorganising to make something simpler or more efficient, or a comfortable excuse.
practiceSentences: The rationalisation cut nine venues to four.
What rationalisation lies behind closing the smaller halls?
Rationalisation can mean efficiency, or a reason invented afterwards.
His rationalisation of missing rehearsal convinced nobody.
One rationalisation reorganises; the other explains away.

words.group: Word building: -al, -ation and -ence
words.childMeaning: A relationship in which each side relies on the other.
practiceSentences: The interdependence of singer and drummer is heard before it is seen.
What interdependence holds this ensemble together?
Interdependence is mutual reliance, not a one-way need.
Their interdependence meant one absence stopped the whole rehearsal.
Interdependence runs both ways; dependence runs one.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: The pattern of stress and pace in ordinary sentences.
practiceSentences: Prose-rhythm is why one paragraph reads faster than another.
What gives this passage its prose-rhythm?
Prose-rhythm exists whether or not a writer attends to it.
She read her draft aloud to hear its prose-rhythm.
Prose-rhythm is unmetred; verse counts its beats.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: The fixed pattern of lines, rhyme and metre a poem follows.
practiceSentences: The verse-form dictates fourteen lines and a turn at the ninth.
Which verse-form does this song lyric borrow?
A verse-form is a constraint the poet chose.
She kept the verse-form and changed everything inside it.
A verse-form has rules; free verse has none to keep.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: Poetry written without regular rhyme or metre.
practiceSentences: Free-verse still uses line breaks, and uses them deliberately.
Why is free-verse harder to write well than it looks?
Free-verse abandons metre, not shape.
The song's lyrics are free-verse set to a strict beat.
Free-verse has no fixed pattern; blank verse keeps the metre and drops the rhyme.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: The overall shape and conventions a poem is built on.
practiceSentences: The poetic-form carries expectations before a word is read.
What poetic-form suits a lament?
A poetic-form is a promise to the reader about what is coming.
She chose a traditional poetic-form for a modern subject.
Poetic-form is the shape; content is what fills it.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: A poem spoken by one character to a silent listener.
practiceSentences: The dramatic-monologue lets the speaker reveal more than he intends.
Who is the silent listener in this dramatic-monologue?
A dramatic-monologue has an audience inside the poem.
Her dramatic-monologue gives the accused her own account at last.
A dramatic-monologue addresses someone; a soliloquy is spoken alone.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: The set of beliefs a person or group uses to judge what matters.
practiceSentences: The two communities share a language and not a value-system.
What value-system does this song assume in its listener?
A value-system is visible in what somebody refuses to do.
Her value-system survived the move and adapted at the edges.
A value-system judges what matters; a rule only says what is allowed.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: Feeling able to speak up without fear of humiliation.
practiceSentences: Psychological-safety is why one rehearsal room produces better ideas.
What creates psychological-safety in a group of strangers?
Psychological-safety means a wrong note can be admitted early.
The conductor built psychological-safety by making her own mistakes public.
Psychological-safety allows disagreement; comfort merely avoids it.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: Exhaustion caused by prolonged stress or overwork.
practiceSentences: Burnout ended more musical careers than any lack of talent.
What early signs of burnout are easiest to ignore?
Burnout builds slowly and arrives suddenly.
The orchestra shortened its season after two years of burnout.
Burnout is exhaustion from overwork; tiredness passes with sleep.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: To do with both social position and income together.
practiceSentences: Access to an instrument is a socioeconomic question before it is a musical one.
What socioeconomic barriers keep children out of the orchestra?
Socioeconomic factors travel together, which is why one word covers both.
The study grouped families by socioeconomic background.
Socioeconomic joins status and income; economic covers only the money.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: Depending on being a citizen of a particular country.
practiceSentences: The scholarship is citizenship-based, so residence is not enough.
Is a citizenship-based rule fair to long-settled families?
A citizenship-based entitlement excludes by status rather than by need.
They replaced the citizenship-based scheme with a residence test.
Citizenship-based turns on nationality; needs-based turns on circumstance.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: The decisions a government makes about how to act.
practiceSentences: Public-policy decided that every school would keep a music room.
What public-policy shaped this festival's funding?
Public-policy is a choice, even when it looks like an absence of one.
Her public-policy work moved from research into legislation.
Public-policy is what a government decides; law is how it binds.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: Basic entitlements every person holds simply by being human.
practiceSentences: Human-rights do not depend on a government granting them.
Which human-rights does this treaty actually enforce?
Human-rights are claimed as universal, which is what makes them contested.
The song became a human-rights anthem in three countries.
Human-rights belong to everyone; civil rights come from a particular state.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: To offset something with an equal force on the other side.
practiceSentences: The bass counterbalances the brightness of the upper voices.
What would counterbalance this section's weight?
To counterbalance is to offset, not to cancel.
She counterbalanced the long slow movement with a brisk finale.
To counterbalance is to weigh against; to remove is to take away.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: To judge or estimate the size, extent or feeling of something.
practiceSentences: It is hard to gauge an audience from the stage.
How would you gauge the reaction to this piece?
To gauge is to estimate carefully, not to guess.
She gauged the room's mood and changed the running order.
A gauge is also the instrument that measures.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: To plan something in detail, step by step.
practiceSentences: They map-out the whole tour before booking a single hall.
How would you map-out a year of rehearsals?
To map-out is to make a plan somebody else could follow.
She likes to map-out an argument before writing the first line.
To map-out is to plan in detail; to sketch is to plan roughly.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: To adjust something so it measures or performs correctly again.
practiceSentences: The tuner had to be recalibrated after the flight.
When would you recalibrate your expectations?
To recalibrate is to correct a drift you may not have noticed.
They recalibrated the plan after the first three concerts.
To recalibrate is to reset a standard; to repair is to fix a fault.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: To express or design something again in a different way.
practiceSentences: She reformulated the question and it suddenly had an answer.
How would you reformulate this claim more carefully?
To reformulate is to change the form and keep the substance.
The committee reformulated the policy three times in a month.
To reformulate is to restate; to rephrase changes only the words.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: To support a learner with structure that is removed as they improve.
practiceSentences: The teacher scaffolds the first two verses and lets go of the third.
What scaffolding does a beginner need to read music?
To scaffold is to plan your own removal.
She scaffolded the task with a worked example and a checklist.
Scaffolding is temporary support; a rule stays in place.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: Making a judgement about worth or quality.
practiceSentences: The final paragraph is evaluative rather than descriptive.
