What evaluative claim is this review actually making?
An evaluative statement needs criteria, stated or assumed.
She separated the evaluative comments from the observations.
Evaluative judges; descriptive reports.

words.group: Words: rhythm, voice and what music carries
words.childMeaning: Done in an orderly, step-by-step way.
practiceSentences: Her methodical practice covered one passage at a time.
What does a methodical approach to learning a score involve?
Methodical work is slower at first and faster in the end.
He was methodical to the point of writing down which fingerings failed.
Methodical follows an order; thorough merely leaves nothing out.

words.group: Grammar: the study of word forms, and of sounds
words.childMeaning: The study of how words are built from smaller parts.
practiceSentences: Morphology explains why "unhappiness" has three parts.
What does morphology tell us about this borrowed word?
Morphology looks inside a word; syntax looks between words.
She used morphology to work out an unfamiliar term's meaning.
In biology, morphology is the study of an organism's form.

words.group: Grammar: the study of word forms, and of sounds
words.childMeaning: The study of the sound system of a language.
practiceSentences: Phonology explains which sound differences a language treats as meaningful.
What phonology makes this song hard to translate?
Phonology studies the system; phonetics studies the sounds themselves.
Her phonology research compared four coastal dialects.
Phonology concerns sound patterns; morphology concerns word parts.

words.group: Words: the arts, and the effect words have
words.childMeaning: Discussing a subject from several sides rather than arguing one.
practiceSentences: A discursive essay weighs both sides before deciding.
Is this piece discursive or persuasive?
A discursive text presents the strongest case for each view.
She chose a discursive form because the evidence was mixed.
Discursive explores; argumentative advocates.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Changing how an organisation works by moving it onto digital systems.
practiceSentences: Digitalisation turned three filing rooms into one server.
What has digitalisation cost the people who ran those rooms?
Digitalisation changes the work, not only the storage.
The hospital's digitalisation took four years and two false starts.
Digitising converts a document; digitalisation changes the whole process.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Using a physical feature, such as a fingerprint, to identify someone.
practiceSentences: Biometric locks read a fingerprint instead of a key.
What happens if biometric data is stolen?
A biometric cannot be changed once it has leaked.
The border post introduced biometric checks last year.
A password can be replaced; a biometric cannot.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: A shared record of transactions that is very hard to alter.
practiceSentences: A blockchain stores each record in a chain that would have to be rewritten whole.
What problem is a blockchain actually solving here?
A blockchain removes the need to trust one central keeper.
The land registry trialled a blockchain and kept the paper copies.
A blockchain makes a record hard to change; it does not make it true.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Making a file smaller so it takes less space to store or send.
practiceSentences: Compression cut the video to a third of its size.
What does this compression throw away?
Lossless compression keeps everything; lossy compression does not.
Heavy compression turned the photograph into visible squares.
Compression saves space and sometimes spends quality.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Turning coded information back into a readable form.
practiceSentences: Decryption needs the key, not merely the method.
How long would decryption take without the key?
Decryption is encryption run backwards, and only with permission.
The archive released the decryption key after fifty years.
Encryption locks the message; decryption opens it.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Working out where a device or person is on the Earth.
practiceSentences: Geolocation put the photograph within ten metres of the harbour.
What geolocation data does this app send?
Geolocation is useful, and it is also a record of where you have been.
She turned geolocation off before posting the picture.
Geolocation finds a position; a map only shows one.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: The ability of different systems to work together.
practiceSentences: Interoperability lets two hospitals read the same record.
Why is interoperability so often promised and so rarely delivered?
Interoperability needs an agreed standard more than it needs good code.
The lack of interoperability cost the project a year.
Interoperability is systems cooperating; compatibility is one fitting another.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Built on written program instructions rather than on ready-made tools.
practiceSentences: The club runs a coding-based course rather than a drag-and-drop one.
Is a coding-based approach harder to start and easier to extend?
A coding-based solution can be changed by anyone who reads it.
They chose a coding-based tool so the school could adapt it.
Coding-based means somebody wrote the instructions rather than clicked them.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Decided by what the measurements show rather than by opinion.
practiceSentences: The timetable change was data-driven and unpopular.
What makes a decision data-driven rather than data-decorated?
A data-driven decision is only as good as the data behind it.
Their data-driven approach found a problem nobody had reported.
Data-driven follows the evidence; evidence-led admits judgement is still involved.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Connected to other computers so information can be shared.
practiceSentences: Every classroom printer is networked to one server.
What becomes possible once a device is networked?
A networked device is reachable, which is its use and its risk.
The networked sensors reported the flood before anyone saw it.
Networked means connected; standalone means it works alone.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Able to be given instructions that change what it does.
practiceSentences: A programmable thermostat learns the week's pattern.
What makes this device programmable rather than merely adjustable?
A programmable machine can do a job nobody designed it for.
The programmable board cost less than the fixed one.
Programmable takes new instructions; automatic only repeats its own.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: A deliberate attempt to damage or break into a computer system.
practiceSentences: The cyberattack shut the booking system for two days.
How would a school notice a cyberattack early?
A cyberattack often begins with one convincing email.
The hospital's cyberattack delayed operations, not just paperwork.
A cyberattack is the event; cybercrime is the offence.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Criminal activity carried out using computers or networks.
practiceSentences: Cybercrime now costs more than many kinds of theft.
What makes cybercrime difficult to prosecute?
Cybercrime crosses borders faster than the law follows.
The unit investigates cybercrime reported by small businesses.
Cybercrime is the category; a cyberattack is one act within it.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Checking that something is correct or meets its requirements.
practiceSentences: Form validation catches the missing digit before the form is sent.
What validation does this data go through?
Validation checks the input; verification checks the result.
Without validation, one wrong date corrupted the whole export.
Validation also means having your feelings acknowledged, which is a different use.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: To do with the waves that carry light, radio and X-rays.
practiceSentences: Radio and visible light are both electromagnetic waves.
Which electromagnetic waves does this device use?
Electromagnetic waves need no material to travel through.
The whole wireless network runs on electromagnetic radiation.
The electromagnetic spectrum runs from radio waves to gamma rays.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Happening at regular intervals, or arranged in repeating patterns.
practiceSentences: The system runs a periodic backup every night.
What periodic checks does this equipment need?
A periodic signal repeats itself at a fixed rate.
The periodic table arranges elements by repeating properties.
Periodic repeats on a schedule; occasional does not.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: The movement of water through a membrane towards the stronger solution.
practiceSentences: Osmosis moves water into the root without any pumping.
In which direction does osmosis carry the water here?
Osmosis needs a membrane that lets water through and not the dissolved substance.
Reverse osmosis is how some plants make drinking water from the sea.
People say they learned something by osmosis, which is a joke about the word.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: The study of living things too small to see without a microscope.
practiceSentences: Microbiology explains why the water had to be boiled.
What can microbiology tell us that a symptom cannot?
Microbiology became possible only once lenses were good enough.
Her work in microbiology traced the outbreak to one well.
Microbiology studies the organisms; medicine treats what they do.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Using letters to stand for numbers in a rule or formula.
practiceSentences: The algebraic expression works for every value of n.
Which algebraic rule describes this pattern?
An algebraic statement says something about all numbers at once.
She wrote the algebraic form and the pattern became obvious.
Algebraic uses letters; arithmetic uses only numbers.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Growing by a multiplying factor each step, so it accelerates.
practiceSentences: Exponential growth looks slow until it suddenly does not.
Is this growth exponential or merely fast?
An exponential curve doubles in a fixed time, again and again.
The number of connected devices grew exponentially for a decade.
Exponential multiplies each step; linear only adds.

words.group: Words: the machinery of a digital life
words.childMeaning: Changing by the same amount each step, so it plots as a straight line.
practiceSentences: The cost is linear: each extra user adds the same amount.
Is this relationship linear across the whole range?
A linear graph is a straight line, whatever its slope.
She fitted a linear model and it held for four years.
Linear adds the same each time; exponential multiplies.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ity
words.childMeaning: Checking that something is true or has been done correctly.
practiceSentences: Verification meant repeating the count with a different observer.
What verification does this claim still need?
Verification asks whether the result is right; validation asks whether the method was.
She built verification into the process rather than adding it afterwards.
A claim without verification is a claim waiting to be checked.

words.group: Word building: -ation and -ity
words.childMeaning: The quality of applying everywhere and to everyone.
practiceSentences: The universality of the finding was never actually tested outside one region.
What would establish the universality of this rule?
Universality is the strongest claim an argument can make and the hardest to hold.
Their universality claim rested on three studies from one continent.
Universality applies everywhere; generality applies widely.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To check a finding by approaching it from several independent directions.
practiceSentences: They triangulated the account with records, photographs and interviews.
How would you triangulate this single source?
To triangulate is to ask whether independent methods agree.
She triangulated the survey with two datasets she had not collected.
To triangulate is to confirm from several angles; to repeat is to try the same one twice.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To judge something again in the light of new information.
practiceSentences: The second season's data forced them to re-evaluate the whole model.
When would you re-evaluate this conclusion?
To re-evaluate is not to retreat; it is to use what arrived late.
She re-evaluated her argument and kept two thirds of it.
To re-evaluate is to weigh again; to reject is to decide once.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To turn an idea into something that can actually be measured.
practiceSentences: They had to operationalise wellbeing before they could survey it.
How would you operationalise fairness in this study?
To operationalise a concept is to decide what will count as it.
Her decision to operationalise poverty by income shaped every result.
Operationalising a term makes it measurable and narrower at once.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To put forward an idea as a starting point for reasoning.
practiceSentences: The paper postulates a link and then tests it.
What does this argument postulate without saying so?
To postulate is to assume openly, which is the honest kind of assumption.
He postulated three conditions and examined each in turn.
To postulate is to propose a starting point; to prove is to finish the work.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To form an idea without firm evidence for it.
practiceSentences: It is fair to speculate as long as you say that is what you are doing.
What would you speculate from these two readings alone?
To speculate is legitimate; to present speculation as finding is not.
She speculated in the discussion and nowhere else in the paper.
To speculate is to guess reasonably; to conclude is to rest on evidence.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To make things follow one agreed form or measure.
practiceSentences: They standardised the recording sheet so the districts could be compared.
What would you standardise before collecting anything?
To standardise is to buy comparability with some local fit.
The standardised test made the schools comparable and the teaching narrower.
To standardise imposes one form; to adapt allows many.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To arrange information into a table.
practiceSentences: Tabulate the results before you attempt any graph.
How would you tabulate three variables at once?
Tabulating data forces you to decide what the columns are.
She tabulated nine seasons of readings on a single page.
To tabulate is to arrange in a table; to summarise is to shorten.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To organise something into an orderly system.
practiceSentences: The archive was systematised over four years of patient work.
How would you systematise a collection this varied?
To systematise is to impose an order somebody else can learn.
They systematised the field notes and found gaps nobody had noticed.
To systematise builds the system; to organise merely tidies.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A line a curve approaches but never quite reaches.
practiceSentences: The curve nears its asymptote without ever touching it.
Which asymptote does this graph approach?
An asymptote describes a limit that is never arrived at.
She drew the asymptote as a dashed line.
An asymptote is approached forever; a maximum is reached.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: An algebraic expression with exactly two terms.
practiceSentences: The binomial x plus three has two terms and no more.
Which binomial appears on both sides here?
A binomial expands into more terms when it is squared.
She used the binomial expansion rather than multiplying it out.
A binomial has two terms; a polynomial may have many.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Describing an expression whose highest power is three.
practiceSentences: A cubic equation can have up to three solutions.
What makes this equation cubic rather than quadratic?
A cubic curve changes direction twice at most.
She plotted the cubic and found all three roots.
Cubic is the third power; quadratic is the second.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Working from the number below the line in a fraction.
practiceSentences: A denominator-based comparison asks what the whole was.
Why is a denominator-based rate fairer than a raw count?
A denominator-based figure tells you out of how many.
They switched to denominator-based reporting and the ranking reversed.
Denominator-based accounts for the total; a raw count does not.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A group of equations that must all be satisfied together.
practiceSentences: The equation-set has one solution that fits every line.
How many unknowns can this equation-set handle?
An equation-set is solved together, not one at a time.
She wrote the equation-set as a matrix and solved it in one step.
An equation-set is solved jointly; a single equation stands alone.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Using statements that one quantity is greater or less than another.
practiceSentences: An inequality-based constraint sets a limit rather than a value.
What does an inequality-based model allow that an equation does not?
An inequality-based answer is a range, not a point.
They wrote the budget rule as an inequality-based condition.
Inequality-based gives a range; equation-based gives an exact value.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A rectangular arrangement of numbers set out in rows and columns.
practiceSentences: The matrix holds four rows and three columns.
Which matrix represents this transformation?
A matrix can carry a whole equation-set in one object.
She multiplied the two matrices in the correct order.
The plural of matrix is matrices.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Not changing at a constant rate, so it does not plot as a straight line.
practiceSentences: The relationship is nonlinear, so doubling the input does not double the result.
What makes this system nonlinear?
A nonlinear system can be stable for years and then move suddenly.
She fitted a nonlinear model once the straight line failed.
Nonlinear changes at a varying rate; linear changes at a steady one.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: An expression made of terms with whole-number powers added together.
practiceSentences: A polynomial can have any number of terms.
What is the degree of this polynomial?
A polynomial's degree is its highest power.
She factorised the polynomial into three brackets.
A polynomial's degree is the highest power it contains.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A function of the form one divided by the variable.
practiceSentences: The reciprocal-function has an asymptote along each axis.
What happens to a reciprocal-function as the input approaches zero?
A reciprocal-function is undefined at zero, which is where its shape comes from.
She sketched the reciprocal-function in both quadrants.
A reciprocal-function divides one by the variable; a linear one multiplies it.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Drawing on more than one field of study at once.
practiceSentences: The project was interdisciplinary: hydrology, economics and oral history together.
What makes a question interdisciplinary rather than merely broad?
Interdisciplinary work is slow because each field checks differently.
Her interdisciplinary training let her read both the data and the interviews.
Interdisciplinary combines fields; multidisciplinary places them side by side.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Shaped by findings from research rather than by habit.
practiceSentences: The new timetable is research-informed and unpopular.
Is this practice research-informed or merely long-established?
Research-informed means the evidence changed the decision.
They rewrote the guidance to be research-informed and cited every source.
Research-informed follows findings; research-mentioning only quotes them.

words.group: Grammar: meaning, and the two marks that shape a sentence
words.childMeaning: The study of meaning in language.
practiceSentences: Semantics asks what a sentence means, not how it is built.
What semantics separates "few" from "a few"?
Semantics is where an argument about words becomes an argument about ideas.
Her thesis on semantics compared two translations of one treaty.
Semantics studies meaning; syntax studies arrangement.

words.group: Grammar: meaning, and the two marks that shape a sentence
words.childMeaning: A punctuation mark introducing a list, explanation or quotation.
practiceSentences: A colon announces that something is about to follow.
Where would a colon improve this sentence?
A colon needs a complete clause in front of it.
She used a colon to set up the definition that followed.
A colon introduces; a semicolon joins.

words.group: Grammar: meaning, and the two marks that shape a sentence
words.childMeaning: A punctuation mark joining two closely related complete clauses.
practiceSentences: A semicolon joins two clauses that could each stand alone.
Would a semicolon or a full stop suit this pair better?
A semicolon signals a closer link than a full stop admits.
She replaced the comma splice with a semicolon.
A semicolon joins equals; a colon introduces what follows.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To use what you know to estimate beyond it.
practiceSentences: From four years of data they extrapolate the fifth.
Can you extrapolate the trend to next year?
To extrapolate far beyond your evidence is to invent.
She extrapolated the cost from the first three months.
Extrapolate reaches past the data; interpolate fills a gap inside it.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To form a clear idea of something in your mind.
practiceSentences: It is hard to conceptualise a number that large.
How would you conceptualise this problem?
To conceptualise is to give a vague idea a shape.
She conceptualised the whole exhibition before drawing anything.
Conceptualising comes before planning, and both come before building.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: An indirect reference to another work, person or event.
practiceSentences: The title is an allusion to an older poem.
Which allusion opens the second stanza?
An allusion rewards the reader who recognises it and does not punish the one who does not.
The speech was full of allusions to the founding story.
An allusion hints at something; a quotation states it.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Placing two things side by side so the contrast shows.
practiceSentences: The juxtaposition of the wedding and the funeral is deliberate.
What does this juxtaposition make you notice?
Juxtaposition argues without saying anything.
The photograph's juxtaposition of new tower and old well says it all.
Juxtaposition places side by side; comparison discusses the difference.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A statement that seems to contradict itself yet holds a truth.
practiceSentences: The more you explain the joke, the less funny it is: that is a paradox.
Which paradox is the poem built around?
A paradox is not a mistake; it is a truth folded awkwardly.
She ended on a paradox and left the audience arguing.
A paradox seems contradictory; a contradiction simply is.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A speech in which a character alone on stage thinks aloud.
practiceSentences: The soliloquy lets the audience hear what nobody else may.
Where does the soliloquy fall in the play?
A soliloquy is spoken alone; an aside is spoken past the others.
His soliloquy runs to forty lines and changes the whole play.
A soliloquy reveals a mind; a dialogue reveals a relationship.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To do with the meaning of words.
practiceSentences: The disagreement was semantic: they meant different things by fair.
What semantic difference separates these two words?
A semantic field groups words that share a subject.
She traced the semantic shift of the word across two centuries.
Semantic is about meaning; syntactic is about arrangement.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: The arrangement of words to make a well-formed sentence.
practiceSentences: The syntax is correct even where the meaning is not.
What does the poet's unusual syntax achieve?
Syntax decides what a sentence can mean before any word is chosen.
Inverted syntax slows a reader down, which may be the point.
Syntax is the order; semantics is the meaning.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A short, sharp saying that makes its point wittily.
practiceSentences: The essay closes on an epigram nobody forgets.
Which epigram would you choose for the title page?
An epigram must be short enough to repeat from memory.
She wrote an epigram where a paragraph had been.
An epigram is witty and brief; a proverb is old and anonymous.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A serious story or event, often ending in sadness or loss.
practiceSentences: Rohan wanted the play's tragedy to feel honest, not exaggerated.
Why does great theatre so often balance tragedy with humour?
"This is a tragedy, not a joke," Ms Dina reminded the nervous cast.
The story ended in tragedy, leaving the audience silent and still.
The flood was a tragedy the village would remember for generations.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To show that two things change together.
practiceSentences: The two sets of readings correlate closely.
Does reading time correlate with the results here?
Two things can correlate without either causing the other.
She correlated the rainfall with the harvest over ten years.
To correlate is to move together; to cause is another claim entirely.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To add a limit to a statement so it is not too broad.
practiceSentences: Qualify the claim before somebody else does it for you.
How would you qualify this conclusion?
To qualify a statement is to make it defensible, not to weaken it.
She qualified every finding with the size of the sample.
Qualify also means to become eligible, as for a competition.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To prove that a statement is wrong.
practiceSentences: One counterexample was enough to refute the rule.
What evidence would refute this claim?
To refute is to disprove, not merely to deny.
He refuted the argument and conceded the conclusion.
Refute needs evidence; reject needs only an opinion.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To support a claim with evidence.
practiceSentences: Substantiate each assertion or remove it.
What would substantiate this figure?
To substantiate is to show the working, not to repeat the claim.
The article failed to substantiate its most quoted sentence.
Substantiate provides evidence; assert provides none.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To name things one by one in order.
practiceSentences: Enumerate the reasons before you rank them.
Can you enumerate the steps in the argument?
To enumerate is to list with a number attached.
She enumerated four objections and answered three.
Enumerate names each one; summarise gathers them together.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: To take an argument or text apart to see how it works.
practiceSentences: Deconstruct the advertisement before you judge it.
How would you deconstruct this opening paragraph?
To deconstruct is to expose the assumptions holding a thing up.
She deconstructed the speech line by line.
To deconstruct is to take apart; to destroy is not the same word.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Cartesian describes the coordinate system that fixes a point with an x and a y value, named after Descartes.
practiceSentences: Plot the shape's corners on the Cartesian plane before you rotate it.
Which quadrant of the Cartesian plane holds a point with two negative values?
The Cartesian system is named after the French thinker René Descartes.
Every point on a Cartesian grid is fixed by just two numbers.
Maps, graphs and computer screens all rely on Cartesian coordinates.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A fixed relationship in which one quantity scales with another.
practiceSentences: The graph shows proportionality between distance and time.
Is there proportionality across the whole range?
Proportionality means doubling one doubles the other.
The recipe relies on proportionality, so it scales to any number.
Proportionality is a constant ratio; correlation need not be.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Describing an expression in which the highest power is two.
practiceSentences: A quadratic equation has at most two solutions.
Which term makes this equation quadratic?
A quadratic graph is a curve, never a straight line.
She solved the quadratic by completing the square.
Quadratic means squared; linear means to the first power.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Happening or being solved at the same time.
practiceSentences: Simultaneous equations are solved together, not one after the other.
What makes these two equations simultaneous?
Two simultaneous equations share a solution that fits both.
The simultaneous broadcasts reached four countries at once.
Simultaneous means at once; consecutive means one then the next.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: A statement in mathematics that has been proved from other truths.
practiceSentences: The theorem holds for every right-angled triangle.
Which theorem would you use here?
A theorem is proved once and then relied on for ever.
She quoted the theorem rather than reproving it.
A theorem is proved; a conjecture is only believed.

words.group: Words: bringing the year together
words.childMeaning: Imagined for the sake of argument rather than real.
practiceSentences: Take a hypothetical class of thirty and work it through.
Is that a hypothetical case or one that happened?
A hypothetical example tests an argument without accusing anyone.
She answered the hypothetical question and refused the real one.
Hypothetical is supposed for argument; theoretical rests on a theory.
